Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Money, work & business

loss noun

losing something

also losses, make a loss, suffer a loss, profit and loss, the loss of someone, waste (of time, money)

classical

Hor. Ep. 1.16.56: damnum est, nōn facinus
Cato Agr. 3.3: damnī nihil erit

damnum, damnī n.

noun, second declension

loss, harm (the opposite of lucrum, gain)

To suffer a loss is damnum facere (Plautus, Cicero; Lewis & Short), not to cause one; Lewis & Short give damnum dare, to inflict one, as ante-classical.

Other words

  • jactūra, jactūrae f. — a loss, a sacrifice (properly, throwing goods overboard)

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 1.12.1: jactūram gravissimam fēcī; Cic. Off. 3.89 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 404

    jactūram facere, to suffer a loss or make a sacrifice.

  • āmissiō, āmissiōnis f. — the losing (of something or someone)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 1.12.1: tantī virī āmissiō; Cic. Fam. 4.3 (Lewis & Short)

    Lewis & Short: several times in Cicero, elsewhere rare. Of a death, as in Pliny.

  • dētrīmentum, dētrīmentī n. — loss, harm, a setback

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Leg. 1.51: propter damna aut dētrīmenta (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • nam dē mīlle fabae modiīs cum surripis ūnum, damnum est, nōn facinus

    for when you steal one peck of beans out of a thousand, it’s a loss, not a crimeHor. Ep. 1.16.55–56

  • sī citō sustuleris et vāsa parāta erunt, damnī nihil erit ex tempestāte

    if you gather them up quickly and have the jars ready, the storm will cost you nothingCato Agr. 3.3

  • Jactūram gravissimam fēcī, sī jactūra dīcenda est tantī virī āmissiō.

    I have suffered a very heavy loss, if the loss of so great a man can be called a loss.Plin. Ep. 1.12.1

See also damage, lose, stuck.
